newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tajiks agree reconciliation commission - Interfax.
newsitem.headline: Tajiks agree reconciliation commission - Interfax.

text.p: The warring sides in Tajikistan's bitter four-year civil war have agreed to a "national reconciliation commission" at peace talks in Moscow, Russia's Interfax news agency said on Monday.

Akbar Turajonzoda, a senior official with the Tajik Islamist opposition, was quoted by Interfax as saying the opposition and Tajikistan's secular government had agreed on the functions and conditions of the commission after difficult negotiations.

The agency quoted Tajik government spokesman Zafar Saidov as saying the commission would bring opposition figures into all levels of government, prepare for a possible referendum on the constitution and possible parliamentary elections during a "transition period".

He said the commission would also prepare for prisoner exchanges, the return of thousands of refugees and rebuilding the shattered Tajik economy. An accord would be signed in Moscow "in the near future".
But it was unclear when elections or a referendum might be held in the war-torn country.
The opposition has in the past made known its desire to see such a commission form the basis of a power-sharing arrangement in the fragile former Soviet republic.
But diplomats have said the government could use the agreement to win time to strengthen its tenuous grip on power.
The rebels control the mountainous, eastern half of Tajikistan, although this includes only around 10 percent of the population.
"The most important thing now is to speed up the realisation of this accord," said Turajonzoda.
Instability in the remote, central Asian republic bordering Afghanistan and China formed the backdrop to the talks in Moscow last week.

Seven United Nations military observers were taken hostage by a Tajik guerrilla group on Friday but released on Saturday. Fighting in the centre of the republic has flared on and off despite a ceasefire agreed earlier this month.
Previous ceasefires have been routinely flouted. A U.N.-sponsored truce reconfirmed last July collapsed almost as soon as it was signed.
Tens of thousands have been killed and many more displaced in the conflict between the government and guerrillas, further complicated by seething regional and clan rivalries.
